title: Everyone has gone astray (Romans 1:18–3:20)
hook: Paul argues that Jew and Gentile alike have missed the mark

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not ashamed, from Paul's letter to strangers in Rome. Your line was someone who belongs to another.

A group chat, late in the evening. Someone starts listing everything wrong with everybody else. The coworker who never refills the coffee. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven. Everyone piles on. Then one friend types a single line: you do that too. Silence. Paul does exactly this to his readers in Rome. Through the rest of his first chapter he describes a world that has turned away from God: greed, envy, gossip, cruelty, people who know better and don't care. You can almost hear the listeners nodding. Yes. Them. And then he turns around and points at the one nodding.
screen: `A LIST OF EVERYONE ELSE'S WRONGS.` → `THE LISTENERS NOD.` → `THEN PAUL TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the turn: "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself." The finger that was pointing out now points back. Paul builds his case in two halves. First, the nations who never had the law of Moses. They still had creation, he says: God's power can be seen in the things that are made. And they had a conscience, a law written on the heart, that sometimes accuses and sometimes excuses. Second, his own people, the Jewish people, who had the law and the promises. Paul is a Jew himself, arguing as an insider: having the law is a gift, he says, but hearing it isn't the same as keeping it. Then he lands it with a string of lines, mostly from the Psalms: "There is none righteous, no, not one." Nobody gets to stand on the balcony and look down. Paul's Greek word for sin is hamartia. Its verb, in older Greek, could mean to miss: a spear thrown that falls short of the target. So sin, for Paul, is not only a list of bad deeds. It's a condition everyone shares, a whole aim that's off. Christians describe how deep that goes in different ways, and those differences are coming in the days ahead. But the text is plain on one thing: Paul isn't sorting the world into good people and bad people. He's putting everyone in the same room. And that's where the good news can start.
screen: `WHOSOEVER THOU ART THAT JUDGEST.` · `CREATION AND CONSCIENCE.` · `THE LAW, HEARD AND NOT KEPT.` · `HAMARTIA: MISSING THE MARK.` · then, large: `THERE IS NONE RIGHTEOUS, NO, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Let yesterday play back slowly, and find one small, real moment where you aimed at kindness, patience or honesty and fell a little short; not the worst thing you've ever done. Name it plainly, without a speech in your own defense and without beating yourself up, and notice that whoever you judged this week has missed too, and so have you: same room. If you pray, bring that one miss to God and leave it there.
Sin. Hamartia in Greek, a word that could mean missing the mark. For Paul, not just bad deeds but a condition everyone shares.
Your line: all of us. Nobody stands on the balcony. That's day three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Some Christians end the day with an examination of conscience: looking back over it, naming where they fell short, and asking God's forgiveness.

notes: The list of wrongs in Romans 1:18–32 includes 1:26–27, which churches read in different ways; the script summarizes the list generally and does not address those verses. Keeper may want to decide whether to mention them.

Hamartia as 'missing the mark': the verb hamartano is used in Homer for missing with a spear. The archery/target gloss is popular and sound for the root, but Paul's usage should not be reduced to it; the script says 'could mean'. Confirm.
Romans 2:14–15 (law written on the heart, conscience accusing or excusing) is paraphrased.
Care taken to present Paul as a Jew arguing as an insider, and to present Jewish possession of the law as a gift (Romans 3:1–2), to avoid anti-Jewish framing.
Romans 3:10–18 is a chain of quotations mainly from the Psalms; confirm the phrasing 'a string of lines from the Psalms' (Isaiah is also quoted in 3:15–17).
